transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Nice to meet you, Doc. Well, I'm here because... man, it's just getting to be too much at work. I'm a construction manager, right? Have been for a long time. Started out right out of high school and worked my way up, so I know this industry inside and out. But what brings me in is... well, I can start a safety briefing with the guys, or sit down in the trailer for a massive plan review, and I go in trying really, really hard to pay attention. I tell myself I need to lock in because guys' safety is on the line, or thousands of dollars in materials. 

But I swear, within minutes, my mind is just completely off on three other job problems. I'll be sitting there looking right at the safety coordinator or staring at the blueprints, but my brain is actually worrying about a concrete delay on the east side, or if the electricians showed up, or where the framing crew went. And because my head is a million miles away, I miss things. I miss things I absolutely know I should have caught. And it's not because I don't know the job, it's just... I can't keep my head in that one spot for more than a couple of minutes before it's bouncing around to every other fire I need to put out on the site. It's incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it's starting to really mess with my stress levels, because I'm always terrified I missed something critical, and I just can't seem to force myself to stay tuned in no matter how hard I try.
Did you have similar problems paying attention or staying focused as a child?

Oh, man, did I ever. Yeah, it’s funny you ask that because my mom actually kept all these old report cards in a box in the attic, and my wife and I were looking through them a couple of years ago when we moved, and it was just... page after page of the exact same comments. I mean, going all the way back to elementary school, right? First grade, second grade, third grade—it didn't matter who the teacher was, the story was always the same. 

They were always telling my parents that I couldn’t stay in my seat. I remember Mrs. Gable in fourth grade actually taped a square around my desk on the floor and told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape during reading time, because I was always up wandering over to the window or checking out what the kid three rows over was doing. And talking out of turn? Forget about it. I’d just blurt out whatever popped into my head. If the teacher asked a question, I didn't even wait to raise my hand, I just yelled out the answer, or sometimes I'd just start talking about a truck I saw on the way to school while she was trying to teach math. 

And the homework... it was a disaster. Half the time I'd do it and then lose it on the way to school, or leave it on the kitchen counter, or it would just vanish into the black hole that was my backpack. My parents tried everything—folders, planners, you name it—but nothing worked. And when it came to classwork, I was always the first one done, but it was because I just rushed through the directions. I'd read the first three words of a worksheet, assume I knew what they wanted, and just scribble down answers before I really even understood what I was supposed to be doing. So I'd get these terrible grades on assignments I actually knew the material for, just because I couldn't slow down enough to read the whole sentence. So, yeah, it’s been going on a long time. It’s just that now, instead of losing a spelling worksheet, I’m worried about losing a fifty-thousand-dollar materials order, you know?
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless lately?

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say depressed or hopeless. Stressed? Absolutely. Out of my mind with stress, like I was saying. I mean, when you're running a crew of fifty guys and the subs are calling you at six in the morning because the lift is broken, and you're already trying to figure out how to cover for the foreman who called out sick... it's a lot. But it's not like a sad feeling, you know? It's more like a constant, buzzing anxiety that I'm dropping the ball. 

My wife, Sarah—she's a saint, really—she sometimes asks me if I'm depressed because I'll come home and just crash on the couch, completely wiped out. I won't even want to go out to the garage and work on my old Chevy, which is usually my favorite thing to do on a Saturday. But I have to explain to her, it's not that I'm sad or don't care about life, it's just that my brain feels like a car engine that's been redlining all day long. By the time I get home, the gas tank is just empty. I'm just physically and mentally exhausted from trying so hard to keep all the plates spinning at work. So, no, I don't feel hopeless. I just feel like I'm working ten times harder than everyone else just to stay afloat, and it's wearing me out. But depressed? No, I wouldn't use that word. Just... overwhelmed, I guess. Really, really overwhelmed.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot more days than not?

No, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier in that sense. I mean, I worry about the job, obviously. Like I said, I'm stressed about dropping the ball at work, missing a detail on a blueprint, or forgetting to call a sub back. I worry about the concrete setting right if it rains, or if the framing inspector is going to find some tiny code violation that sets us back three days. But that's all just... work stuff, you know? It's tied to the fact that my brain won't focus when I need it to. 

It's not like I'm sitting around worrying about, I don't know, my health, or the economy, or if the sky is falling. I don't lay awake at night chewing on random anxieties. Usually, I hit the pillow and I'm out cold because I'm so exhausted from fighting my own head all day. Sarah, my wife, she's more the worrier type. She'll fret about whether we're saving enough for retirement or if the roof on the house is going to make it through another winter. And I'm just like, "Babe, I can't even think about the roof right now, I'm just trying to make sure I don't screw up this fifty-unit townhome project." So, yeah, no general worrying. Just the stress of trying to keep my head above water at work because I can't seem to lock in on anything for more than five minutes.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

No, no, definitely not. Like I was saying a minute ago about my old Chevy—it's a '69 C10, stepside, I've been restoring it for a few years now—I still absolutely love that thing. I mean, I'll be sitting in my truck at the job site on a Wednesday, eating a sandwich for lunch, and I'm daydreaming about getting the engine block pulled or watching YouTube videos on my phone about how to rebuild the carburetor. I still get really excited about it. The interest is definitely still there, a hundred percent. 

It's just... well, like I said, it's an energy thing. When the weekend actually hits, I'm either just completely physically shot from running around the site all week, or I'll go out to the garage, realize I can't find my 10-millimeter socket, start tearing apart my tool chest looking for it, find an old weed whacker that I meant to fix last summer, and before I know it, the whole afternoon is gone and I haven't even touched the truck. 

But it's not because I don't care about it anymore. If I had the energy and could actually just get myself to focus on the one task, I'd be under the hood every single night. Same goes for, you know, having a beer and watching the game with my buddies on a Sunday. I still enjoy all of it. I still want to do all of it. I just don't always have the gas left in the tank to actually make it happen, or my brain just gets too scattered to follow through. But the actual enjoyment? No, that hasn't changed at all. I definitely still love the stuff I've always loved.
Have you had trouble with attention or staying focused since childhood?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, this isn't exactly a new thing for me, it's just... it's gotten harder to manage now because the stakes are so much higher with the job and the crew. But if you ask my mom, she’ll tell you this goes all the way back to day one. 

Like, back in elementary school—I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was always pulling my parents aside. They’d have these parent-teacher conferences and it was always the exact same story. Teachers were already telling my parents back then that I just couldn’t stay in my seat. Like, I’d physically be up and wandering around to look at the pencil sharpener or check on the class hamster while she was right in the middle of teaching math. And the talking—man, I was always talking out of turn. I’d just blurt out whatever popped into my head because it felt like I couldn't physically hold the thought in. 

And the homework, forget about it. I’d actually do the homework sometimes, sitting at the kitchen table while my mom watched me like a hawk, but then I'd shove it in my backpack and somehow, between the front door of my house and my desk at school, it would just vanish into a black hole. Lost it all the time. My backpack was just a graveyard of crumpled papers. 

Or we'd get a worksheet or a project, and I’d just rush right through the directions. I'd be halfway done with the page before I even really understood what we were supposed to be doing, and then I'd get it all wrong because I didn't actually read the instructions. I remember one time in fifth grade, we were supposed to be building these little dioramas, and I was so excited about it, but I rushed the instructions so bad I glued the whole box together backward and had to start over. 

My dad used to get so frustrated with me. He’s an old-school guy, you know? Worked in a machine shop his whole life. He just thought I wasn't applying myself, or that I was being disrespectful or lazy. But I wasn't trying to be a bad kid. I just... my brain was always going a hundred miles an hour, even back then. It's like, I've always been this way. Always moving, always missing the details, always getting ten steps ahead of myself before I know where I'm going. So, yeah, it's definitely been a lifelong thing. It's not just a recent stress thing from the sites, even though the stress definitely makes it a hundred times worse now. But back then, it was just... well, they just called me a handful.
Before age 12, did these attention or restlessness problems cause trouble in more than one setting, like both at school and at home?

Yeah, it was everywhere. It wasn't just a school thing. Like I was saying about my dad, at home it was a constant battle. I would be told to clean the garage or take out the trash, and I would get halfway to the driveway, see a stray baseball, start throwing it against the wall, and completely forget the trash until my dad came out yelling. So it was definitely both home and school back then. 

And honestly, doc, it is the exact same story today, just with adult consequences. It is still bleeding into every single part of my life. Like at work right now, it has gotten bad enough that it is not just me being stressed internally, it is actually causing real, tangible problems. The missed follow-ups are killing me. I will have a superintendent ask me to confirm a lumber delivery, and I swear I will do it, but then a guy asks me a question about the grading, and the lumber is just gone from my brain. My site coordination has been so poorly organized lately that my employer actually had to step in. They pulled me aside and gave me a formal expression of concern. A literal sit-down where they told me my disorganization is costing time and money. That is a terrible feeling, sitting there knowing you are messing up but not knowing how to stop your brain from doing it. 

Then I drive home, and I do not even get a break from it there, because it is affecting my marriage, too. Sarah, my wife, she is just completely worn down from it. I will tell her I will handle calling the bank about the mortgage, or I will fix the gutters this weekend. I mean it when I say it. I really do. But then the weekend comes, and I get sidetracked in the garage, like I told you, and I do not do the thing I said I would handle. So she has to remind me. And then remind me again on Tuesday. By Thursday, she is just exhausted from having to constantly manage me like I am one of the kids. It is exhausting for her, and it makes me feel like a lousy husband. So, yeah, childhood, adulthood, it does not matter. It is always messing me up in more than one place at a time.
